title: Future-sin blanket remission would call David pardoned while compounding adultery and Uriah’s murder
source_text: XXII. Praeterea neminem poenitere potest peccati quod nondum admissum est. Sed sine poenitentia peccatum remitti non potest, & ut aliquis peccati veniam a Deo impetret, necesse est ut prius peccati poenitentia ducatur. Neque potest aliquis solvi reatu peccati illius in quo perseverat, & a quo recedendi propositum non habet. Sed si peccata omnia futura simul remittuntur ei qui se ad Deum convertit, homini qui semel ad Deum conversus est omnia peccata, quantumlibet gravia, in quae postea labitur, censeri debent illi remissa esse, etiam quum illa committit, & tantum a vera poenitentia abest, ut peccatum peccato graviori cumulet. Exempli gratia, censeri debebit remissum fuisse Davidi adulterium cum uxore Uriae, etiam quum non solum in adulterio illo persistebat, sed ipsius Uriae mortem machinabatur, & illum in ebrietatem impellere tentabat, & proditorie illi blandiebatur. Adeoque dicendum erit, Davidem in eo statu non fuisse morti aeternae obnoxium, sed acceptum Deo ad vitam aeternam, & idoneum qui regnum coelorum ingrederetur, & ita falsum esse, quod Scriptura per os Joannis pronunciat, Qui non diligit manet in morte. Et scitis quoniam omnis homicida non habet vitam aeternam in semetipso manentem. Nisi quis dicere velit, Davidem proximum suum sicut ad salutem oportet dilexisse, dum uxorem ejus constuprabat, & injuste mortem illi moliebatur. Aut peccata illi actu esse remissa, qui tamen manet mortis aeternae reus, & merito suo vita aeterna excludendus, si mors illum deprehenderet: a quibus abhorret communis Christianorum sensus.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover no one can repent of a sin not yet admitted. But without repentance a sin cannot be remitted, and for someone to obtain pardon of sin from God it is necessary that he first be led by repentance of sin. Nor can anyone be loosed from the guilt of that sin in which he perseveres and from which he has no purpose of withdrawing. But if all future sins are remitted at once to him who converts himself to God, then to the man once converted to God all sins, however grave, into which he later falls ought to be reckoned remitted to him even while he commits them and is so far from true repentance that he heaps sin upon heavier sin. For example, David’s adultery with Uriah’s wife would have to be reckoned remitted even while he not only persisted in that adultery but plotted Uriah’s death, tried to drive him into drunkenness, and treacherously flattered him. And so it would have to be said that David in that state was not liable to eternal death but accepted by God unto eternal life and fit to enter the kingdom of heaven—and thus that what Scripture pronounces through John’s mouth is false: Whoever does not love remains in death. And you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in himself. Unless someone should wish to say that David loved his neighbor as salvation requires while he was corrupting his wife and unjustly plotting his death; or that sins are actually remitted to him who nevertheless remains guilty of eternal death and by his desert to be shut out from eternal life if death should seize him—from which the common sense of Christians recoils.
pass_b_english: No repentance of uncommitted sin → no remission; persevering sinners stay bound.
Blanket future-pardon would bless David mid-adultery and Uriah-plot—against 1 John and Christian sense.
